builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
summary: The method replaces generic approval instructions (e.g., 'Some actions need approval') in agent system prompts with provenance guidance stating where requirements originate, preventing the agent from hallucinating unsupported permissions in self-written context summaries. It costs only a system prompt modification—no additional infrastructure, memory, or latency overhead. Failure modes include residual unsupported restrictions (0.3% held-out rate) and fragile mitigation of unsupported authorizations, which showed inconsistent effects across held-out sets (17 to 11 of 48 runs).
rationale: This is a zero-cost prompt engineering intervention that significantly reduces unsafe permission hallucinations in long-running agents, fitting constrained infrastructure without requiring model retraining or additional compute.
technique: Provenance-aware system prompts for agent handoffs

claims.statement: The method replaces generic approval instructions (e.g., 'Some actions need approval') in agent system prompts with provenance guidance stating where requirements originate, preventing the agent from hallucinating unsupported permissions in self-written context summaries. It costs only a system prompt modification—no additional infrastructure, memory, or latency overhead. Failure modes include residual unsupported restrictions (0.3% held-out rate) and fragile mitigation of unsupported authorizations, which showed inconsistent effects across held-out sets (17 to 11 of 48 runs).

Replacing a generic approval instruction with provenance guidance cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and from 1.8% to 0.3% on held-out templates (both p < 10^-9), without materially affecting required approval requests.
